title_en: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are
title_ru: Как телефон узнаёт, где вы находитесь
description_ru: Как работает спутниковая навигация: радиосигналы, атомные часы и поправки теории относительности, без которых карта ошибалась бы на километры.
text:
When a map on your phone shows a blue dot that moves as you walk down the street, it seems like a simple trick. In reality, that dot depends on one of the most sophisticated systems ever built, involving dozens of satellites, clocks that lose less than a second in millions of years and, surprisingly, Albert Einstein. The technology is known as the Global Positioning System, or GPS, and understanding it requires only a few key ideas.

The system was developed by the United States military during the 1970s and 1980s and was fully operational in the mid-1990s. At first, civilians were allowed to use it only with deliberately reduced accuracy, but this restriction was removed in 2000, and an industry worth billions was born. Today, GPS is one of several satellite navigation systems. Europe operates Galileo, Russia has GLONASS and China runs BeiDou, and most modern phones can combine signals from all of them.

At any moment, about thirty working GPS satellites are circling the Earth at a height of roughly twenty thousand kilometres. Each one completes two orbits per day, and they are arranged so that at least four are visible from almost any point on the planet. The satellites do not receive anything from your phone. They simply broadcast a continuous radio signal, which contains two pieces of information: where the satellite is, and exactly what time the signal was sent.

The ground also plays a part. Control stations scattered around the world monitor every satellite, measure its exact position and clock error, and send corrections up to it several times a day. Without this constant supervision, small mistakes in the orbits would slowly accumulate, and the position of your blue dot would drift by metres, then by tens of metres. It is a reminder that even the most automatic technology depends on a great many people working quietly in the background.

Your phone listens to these signals and measures how long each one took to arrive. Because radio waves travel at the speed of light, which is about three hundred thousand kilometres per second, the delay can be converted into a distance. If a signal took about seventy milliseconds, the satellite is about twenty thousand kilometres away. A single distance, however, places you only somewhere on the surface of an enormous imaginary sphere around the satellite.

A second satellite gives a second sphere, and the two spheres intersect in a circle. A third sphere narrows it down to just two points, one of which is usually in space and can be ignored. This method is called trilateration, and it is different from triangulation, which uses angles rather than distances. In theory, three satellites are enough, but in practice a fourth is needed, and the reason is a matter of timing.

The difficulty is that light is extremely fast. In one millionth of a second, a radio signal travels about three hundred metres, so to find your position within a few metres, the phone must measure time with an accuracy of a few billionths of a second. The satellites carry atomic clocks, which are astonishingly precise, but a phone cannot afford one. Instead, it uses the fourth satellite to correct its own cheap clock, treating the time error as one more unknown to be calculated.

Now comes the part that involves Einstein. According to his theory of special relativity, a moving clock runs slightly slower, and the satellites travel at about fourteen thousand kilometres per hour, so their clocks lose roughly seven millionths of a second each day. General relativity predicts the opposite effect: clocks run faster where gravity is weaker, and at that altitude, the satellite clocks gain about forty-five millionths of a second per day.

The net result is that the clocks in orbit run about thirty-eight microseconds per day faster than clocks on the ground. This may sound trivial, but if it were ignored, the position errors would grow by about ten kilometres every day, and the system would be useless within hours. To prevent this, engineers set the satellite clocks to tick slightly slower before launch, so that they match time on Earth once they are in orbit. In this way, GPS has become a daily test of relativity.

There are other complications. The signal slows down when it passes through the atmosphere, and it can bounce off tall buildings, which is why your dot sometimes jumps to the wrong street in a city centre. Modern phones reduce such problems by combining satellite data with information from mobile masts, wireless networks and motion sensors. The typical accuracy of a phone outdoors is about five metres, and specialised equipment can reach a few centimetres.

The next time your phone helps you find a restaurant, it may be worth remembering what lies behind the blue dot: a constellation of satellites, a few billionths of a second, and a physicist who, more than a hundred years ago, claimed that time itself is not the same for everybody. It is rare for an abstract idea to become so practical that millions of people rely on it every day without even noticing.
